title: Design Authentication Manager
statement:
Design an authentication manager that tracks session tokens. Every token lives for exactly `ttl` time units after it is created or last renewed. The manager supports three operations; each operation carries the current time `t`.

- `generate <tokenId> <t>`: create a new token `tokenId`, which expires at time `t + ttl`. The id has never been generated before.
- `renew <tokenId> <t>`: if the token exists and is **unexpired** at time `t`, set its expiry to `t + ttl`. If the token does not exist or has already expired, do nothing.
- `count <t>`: output the number of tokens that are unexpired at time `t`.

A token with expiry `e` is unexpired at time `t` exactly when `e > t`; a token whose expiry equals `t` is already expired and can no longer be renewed. The times of successive operations are strictly increasing.

Process the operations in order and print the answer of every `count`. The number of operations can reach `10^5`, so scanning every token on each `count` is too slow.

**Follow-up:** implement this as a class with `generate`, `renew` and `countUnexpiredTokens` methods. A hash map from token to expiry combined with a min-heap of expiry times (or a queue, since expiries are created in increasing order) lets expired tokens be dropped lazily before each operation.
inputFormat:
The first line contains two integers `q` and `ttl`.
Each of the next `q` lines is one operation: `generate <tokenId> <t>`, `renew <tokenId> <t>` or `count <t>`.
outputFormat: For every `count` operation, in order, print one line with its answer. At least one `count` operation is present.

examples.input:
7 5
generate aaa 1
renew aaa 2
generate bbb 3
count 6
count 7
renew aaa 8
count 8
examples.explanation: aaa expires at 6, is renewed at time 2 to expire at 7; bbb expires at 8. At time 6 both are alive (2). At time 7 aaa has expired, bbb is alive (1). The renew at 8 is ignored because aaa is expired, and at time 8 bbb is expired too (0).

examples.input:
6 3
generate x 1
renew x 4
count 4
generate y 5
renew y 7
count 9
examples.explanation: x expires at 4, so the renew at time 4 is ignored and count 4 is 0. y expires at 8 but is renewed at 7 to expire at 10, so at time 9 it is still alive.

hints: Keep a hash map from tokenId to its current expiry time. Scanning the whole map on every count is what makes the naive solution too slow.
Expired tokens can be discarded lazily: before handling an operation at time t, remove tokens whose expiry is at most t. A min-heap of (expiry, tokenId) pairs finds them quickly.
A renew leaves a stale heap entry behind. When popping, only delete the token if the popped expiry still equals the expiry stored in the map.
